correctness.rationale: An independent census builds rooted trees by multiset decomposition of child branches, then uses the unique centroid or unordered pair of centroid halves to get each unrooted shape once. A tree has a unique centroid precisely when every branch there has fewer than half the vertices; in the bicentroid case the middle edge cuts two equal halves. For each root the signed −L columns are updated by summing edge differences. A division-free subset expansion of the determinant reproduces all nine rows of the exact zero/unit/nonunit table over 749 instances. At order nine the counts are 361/60/2, and both nonunit cases belong to one shape. On the displayed labels both roots 2,3 have determinant −2, and the displayed permutation exchanges them. The asserted parity vector annihilates all columns for root 2 modulo two; the parity kernel and full-rank column lattice both have index two and hence coincide. Integer Cayley–Hamilton expresses each later column in the first nine columns with integer coefficients, so allowing longer horizons does not remove the obstruction.
residual_risks: Sign is relative to the displayed vertex order and column convention; the absolute determinant and lattice index are invariant. ‘Half’ means one of the two parity cosets is excluded. Only unit-edge trees and signed integer inputs are covered.

value.rationale: The cutoff measures the first point at which ordinary real controllability ceases to guarantee exact integer-input reachability for a natural family of unit-network systems. Locating the single minimal shape, both actuators, and an explicit parity test explains the difference rather than supplying an arbitrary small spectral census. The result serves as a sharp counterexample for general unimodularity conjectures about Laplacian input columns.
residual_risks: Not an infinite classification or a claim about weighted, multi-input, or magnitude-limited control.
